meta.title: A Foundation Model Assessment for State-of-Health Prediction in Space Li-Ion Batteries
meta.authorsHtml: Roberto Giovanni Sbarra<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Michele Pasquali<sup>1</sup>, Giuliano Coppotelli<sup>1</sup>, Paolo Gaudenzi<sup>1</sup>, Davide di Ienno<sup>2</sup>, Carlo Ciancarelli<sup>2</sup>, Gianluca Furano<sup>3</sup>

abstract: Space applications pose unique challenges to electrochemical systems, making lithium-ion batteries highly nonlinear systems subject to complex degradation mechanisms driven by extreme operating and environmental conditions. In this context, it is essential to develop reliable tools to support mission operations, capable of accurately predicting the evolution of the State of Health (SOH). However, the limited availability of labeled data from past missions and the high variability of operating profiles make SOH prediction particularly complex. To address these issues, this work investigates the use of a pre-trained time-series foundation model that leverages knowledge learned from large-scale time-series data to enable strong generalization capabilities even under operating conditions not observed during model development. The experimental results show that the proposed model achieves high predictive accuracy while maintaining the ability to provide confidence bands on the estimates. This highlights its potential for practical applications in battery health management and decision support in space. The feasibility and validity of the method are demonstrated using an experimental dataset of lithiumion batteries from the NASA Prognostics Center.

blocks.html: Space infrastructure has become a pillar of modern society, supporting essential services such as global communications, Earth observation, navigation, environmental monitoring, and security-related applications. In this rapidly evolving scenario, which sees the proliferation of large constellations comprising tens to thousands of spacecraft, ensuring the continuity of space-based services has become a fundamental requirement [1]. This shift has stimulated the interest in predicting the degradation of space systems. For manufacturers, accurate degradation forecasting helps avoid excessive design margins and reduce the over-engineering traditionally required to safeguard mission lifetimes. For operators, reliable health monitoring enhances autonomous fleet management, supports replacement planning, and ultimately improves decision-making related to the extension of mission operational life [2].

In this context, the Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS) is a mission-critical element of the satellite, as it directly determines the availability of the energy necessary for the operation of all on-board subsystems. Any degradation or failure in the EPS has an immediate impact on mission operations and can lead to irreversible loss of service [3].

At the core of the EPS, lithium-ion batteries play a crucial role, enabling energy storage and power delivery during eclipses and peaks in energy demand. Nevertheless, battery degradation is intrinsically non-linear, strongly influenced by multiple factors, including depth of discharge, charging and discharging regimes, thermal conditions, radiation environment, and specific operating profiles. Consequently, reliable estimation and prediction of the State of Health (SOH) of batteries is a fundamental requirement for the operation and safety of space missions [4].

In recent years, numerous techniques have been proposed for SOH prediction. Advances in Machine Learning have fostered the development of data-driven methods that leverage historical aging data to model degradation and obtain accurate estimates. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have significantly improved predictive capabilities: Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs) model complex nonlinear relationships, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) extract hidden local features from raw data, and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) use information from previous time steps to influence current predictions. Recent studies also highlight the advantages of hybrid approaches, such as CNN-RNN, which can capture both intra-cycle dynamics and long-term degradation trends [5].

However, the limited availability of labeled data from past missions and the high variability of operating profiles make the problem particularly complex. Furthermore, the unique nature of space scenarios and the combined influence of multiple factors make it difficult to develop general mission support tools: even cells tested under nominally identical conditions can show significantly different degradation trajectories [6].

To address these critical issues, this work investigates the use of the Chronos-2 time-series foundation model, developed by Amazon, for direct forecasting of battery SOH. Chronos-2 has consistently outperformed the existing foundation models, demonstrating the effectiveness of in-context learning for improving predictive performance on different types of tasks [7]. The model is evaluated in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training or finetuning, to assess its intrinsic generalization capability across different cells and operating conditions. This approach is especially useful for space missions because it is impossible to train a model on satellites that have not been launched yet and it would be too expensive to replicate the exact radiation and thermal conditions in space in a laboratory. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first application of Chronos-2 to battery health prediction. A sensitivity analysis was performed with respect to the amount of SOH available during the observation phase, evaluating the impact on predictive capacity for increasing forecast horizons. Additionally, a set of signal-based metrics is introduced to investigate the relationship between forecasting accuracy and local signal properties, providing insights into the factors governing prediction variability. The feasibility and reliability of the proposed approach are validated using an experimental dataset of lithium-ion batteries from the NASA Prognostics Center [8], considering different operating profiles representative of mission conditions.

The NASA Ames Prognostics Center of Excellence (PCoE) [8] dataset comprises laboratory tests carried out on 1850 commercial Li-ion cells in different sets. Each set differs from the others due to the varying operating conditions applied during testing. Repeated charge and discharge cycles result in accelerated aging of the batteries, enabling this dataset to be used for SOH estimation and prediction. The experiments were stopped when the batteries reached the end-of-life (EOL) criteria (30% or 20% fade in rated capacity). To test the generalization capabilities of the developed algorithm, two distinct operating conditions differing in temperature and current discharge level, are selected. blocks.html: Chronos-2 is a pretrained universal time-series forecasting model capable of handling univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting tasks in a zero-shot manner [7]. Its group-attention mechanism enables flexible in-context learning across related series, allowing the model to infer multivariate dependencies and effectively exploit both past-only and known future covariates. Chronos-2 is trained on a combination of real univariate datasets and a large corpus of synthetic multivariate time series. This synthetic component is essential to expose the model to various seasonal patterns, causal relationships, and interactions between variables. Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on fev-bench [9], GIFT-Eval [10], and Chronos Benchmark II [11]. These characteristics make it suitable for battery SOH forecasting, where multiple sensor measurements, operational conditions, and long-term degradation trends must be interpreted together to produce reliable and uncertainty-aware predictions.

To systematically investigate the factors that influence the accuracy of SOH predictions, we analyze both the predictive performance of the model and intrinsic properties of the battery degradation signals. The performance is evaluated using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), which quantifies the average deviation between predicted and observed SOH trajectories [12]. Additionally, the Spearman correlation coefficient [13] is employed to assess monotonic relationships between forecast errors and signal characteristics across different cells and prediction horizons (percentage of cycles forecasted until end-of-life) [14]. The characterization of the SOH trajectories properties is performed using four signal-based metrics:

• Sample Entropy (SE): measures the complexity and predictability of the signal. More complex or irregular series tend to have higher SE values, indicating lower repetitiveness. To avoid bias due to the length of the series, each segment was rescaled to a fixed length [15].

• Slope Shift: measures the difference in slope (the coefficient of the linear term in a polynomial fit) between the context and the future portion. Significant variation indicates a change in the signal’s trend that the model must extrapolate, potentially increasing the error [16].

• Curvature Shift: measures the difference in curvature (the coefficient of the quadratic term in a polynomial fit) between the context and the future. It indicates variations in the "shape" of the signal, such as accelerations or decelerations of degradation [16].
• Wasserstein distance: measure of how much the distribution of values in the context differs from that of the future portion. High values indicate a substantial
change in the data distribution that the model must predict [17].

A performance evaluation was carried out using Chronos-2 as a univariate model to estimate the SOH over a certain number of cycles. This approach was adopted to analyze the model’s ability to operate in a domain for which it was not directly trained, using only the foundation model. The analysis was performed on seven cells selected to cover different degradation regimes, including non-stationary behavior, high non-linear levels, and capacity regeneration phenomena.

To analyze predictive robustness, performance was evaluated in terms of MAE over three prediction horizons: 30% (i.e., 70% of the cycle data was used as context to predict the remaining 30%), 50% and 70%, corresponding to an increasing level of difficulty of the problem.

blocks.html: It is possible to observe how the algorithm generally achieves a high level of accuracy for the various cells and for the different prediction horizons. In particular, the best results for the 30% and 50% horizons are achieved in cell B36, with an error of less than 1%, while the best result for the 70% horizon is obtained in cell B06, with an error of around 1.6%.

Figures 1 and 2 show the best results for the 50% and 70% horizons. It can be seen that the algorithm does not present a narrow uncertainty band when propagating for a number of cycles equal to those in the known context, showing a mean solution very close to the real one. In the case of the 70% horizon, it can be seen that, despite the average solution remaining good, the uncertainty band widens progressively, precisely because the information available from the context is less than that necessary for the prediction.

blocks.html: For the 30% horizon, the MAE consistently remains below 5%. The worst cases are evident for the 50% horizon, with cell B18 reaching an error of 7%, and for the 70% horizon, with cell B05 reaching 12%. Figures 3 and 4 show the two cases just mentioned. In the case of 50%, despite having an error higher than the average, the ground truth solution remains within the uncertainty band for most points. In the case of 70%, however, the algorithm fails to correctly predict the change in curvature, resulting in a significantly higher error and a confidence interval that, despite widening, does not contain the ground truth solution, highlighting the potential need for an approach based on covariates or physical modeling.

By analyzing the mean MAE values for each forecasting horizon, it is possible to observe how performance deteriorates with an increase in the amount of data to be predicted (and with a decrease in the amount of information provided to the model as context). In particular, the mean MAE value increases with its dispersion, as expected. However, it is important to note that these observations refer to the mean error across the different cells and do not capture the variability present at the level of the individual cell. Figure 5 shows a bar plot that highlights this variability of the MAE. There is indeed a strong heterogeneity in performance when the horizon and cell changes.

To understand the possible causes of this variability in error, four signal metrics were considered: sample entropy, slope shift, curvature shift, Wasserstein distance. These metrics allow us to characterize the signal in terms of complexity, local dynamics, and global changes in distribution. A correlation analysis was performed between MAE and the considered signal metrics. The strength of the correlation was interpreted according to commonly adopted guidelines, where coefficients between 0.10 and 0.39 indicate weak correlation, 0.40–0.69 moderate correlation, and values above 0.70 strong correlation [13].

blocks.html: The result in Figure 6 shows that there is a weak correlation between the MAE and the intrinsic complexity of the signal, the shift in curvature, and the distance between distributions. Meanwhile, a moderate correlation is achieved for the slope of the signal. This suggests that the strong error heterogeneity does not depend as much on the intrinsic difficulty of the prediction as on model bias, due to the fact that some degradation behaviors fall outside the observed domain during training.

The moderate correlation between the shift in slope and MAE suggests that Chronos produces more accurate predictions when the provided context’s trend is representative of future dynamics. Higher errors and wider uncertainty bands emerge when the model must extrapolate beyond the known domain.

This highlights the potential need for adapting or finetuning the model to new cells, introducing covariates or additional physical information to guide the prediction or using of hybrid models that combine data and physical knowledge to reduce bias in more extensive predictions.

The results show that Chronos-2 is generally capable of accurately predicting the health status of different cells and for different predictive horizons, even when operating in a zero-shot univariate configuration, without specific adaptation to the data under examination.

This behavior highlights the model’s significant generalization capacity, as it captures structural regularities in the degradation process. In the context of space missions, characterized by limited data availability and non-reproducible operating conditions, this property is of great interest. The model’s ability to perform well on unobserved data suggests the presence of structural biases useful for representing common degradation dynamics, making the approach promising for operational support.

blocks.html: At the same time, the analysis shows that accuracy is not directly explainable through standard measures of signal complexity, dynamic variation, or statistical shift between past and future. The model’s performance appears to be primarily governed by the compatibility between the real dynamics and the structures learned during pre-training, highlighting an interpretive limitation of the purely data-driven approach. Predictive robustness is not accompanied by an analogous explanatory robustness, making further methodological development necessary.

In light of these observations, introducing covariates representative of the system’s operational state (Depth of Discharge, temperature, required power, and mission parameters) could reduce the ambiguity of the predictive problem and improve transferability between scenarios. Furthermore, integrating with electrochemical or circuit models could combine predictive accuracy and physical interpretability, a prerequisite for use in critical systems.
